My main complaint (one of several, really) is related to yours. As part of his general introduction of the hierarchy concept into his "continuation" of the existentialist project, he introduces implicitly the notion of "bottom up" complexity. Basically, any attribution of certain kinds of power to individuals wielding that power over a large group tends - according to Jordan - to be irrational, i.e. always some form of externalizing one's locus of control. In other words, much of what we do here at Voat becomes conspiracy in the common language, and in Jordan's language, an inability to appreciate or comprehend the massive complexity inherent in large hierarchically structured groups.

This simply doesn't jibe with history or what I consider accurate sociological models. I agree with Jordan about the existence of hierarchies, but I disagree with him on the nature of the information flow within them - once they become large enough. At that point, I believe top-down communication is the primary driver of behavioral feedback. I get very frustrated with many of Jordan's followers who seem to think that overall outcomes at the tops of hierarchies are somehow always the result of massively complex happenings at the bottom. In fact, it's contradicts pretty much everything else Jordan says about hierarchies. As far as I'm concerned, it amounts to gate keeping.

It should be said, I wouldn't try to downplay the importance of individuality either. I think it is very important, but what has been said about it that was important, was said by Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Dostoevsky, Heidegger, Jaspers, Buber, Marcel, Camus...etc. Jordan has not really advanced the existentialist project in my opinion, although he could perhaps be credited with adding "a little juice" back into something that was dying. To his discredit, I think the way he has enlivened existentialism will be more damaging to it in the long run. His philosophy, from what I gather, is pretty fragmented. 12 Rules was all over the place, and a sort of existentialism for a modern "blog" culture, which his antecedents in the tradition probably would have hated.
